titleStmt.title: On the Decomposition-based Global EDF Scheduling of Parallel Real-Time Tasks †

analytic.title: On the Decomposition-based Global EDF Scheduling of Parallel Real-Time Tasks †

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems are shifting from single-core to multi-core processors, on which software must be parallelized to fully utilize the additional computation power. Recently different types of scheduling algorithms and analysis techniques have been proposed for parallel real-time tasks modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAG). However, this field is still much less mature than traditional real-time scheduling of sequential tasks. In this paper, we study the decomposition-based scheduling for parallel real-time tasks, where a task graph is transferred to a set of independent sporadic tasks. In particular, we proposed a new decomposition strategy that better explores the feature of each task, represented by its structure characteristic value, to improve schedulability. The structure characteristic values do not only provide a clear guidance in task decomposition, but also can be directly used for schedulability tests, as well as to quantify the suboptimality of our scheduling algorithm in terms of capacity augmentation bounds. We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate the real-time performance of our proposed scheduling algorithm, against the state-of-the-art scheduling and analysis methods of different types. Experiment results show that our method consistently outperforms all of the previous methods under different parameter settings.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems are becoming more and more computationally demanding, to meet the ever increasing requirements for the functionality and service quality of embedded systems. Multi-core processors are essential to fulfill this demand. However, using multi-core processors is not a free lunch. Software must be properly parallelized to fully exploit the computation capacity of multi-core processors. However, research in realtime scheduling traditionally assumes sequential workload. Existing scheduling and analysis techniques are hard to be migrated to parallel workload setting and it requires new insights, theories and techniques to address the challenges in parallel real-time software development.

A parallel real-time task can usually be modeled as a Directed acyclic graph (DAG), where edges describe the interdependency constraints among the workload represented by vertices. Real-time scheduling algorithms for DAG task models can be classified into three paradigms: (1) decompositionbased scheduling [1]- [3], (2) global scheduling (without decomposition) [4]- [6] , and (3) federated scheduling [7]- [9] (see Section VI for a review of these scheduling techniques). Among these algorithms, some has shown superiority to others with certain analysis techniques and evaluation metrics. However, overall, the potential of each of these paradigms has not yet been fully exploited, and none of them can claim itself to be a clear winner.

This paper focuses on the decomposition-based scheduling paradigm, in which each DAG task is transferred into a set of independent sporadic tasks, inserting artificial release times and deadlines for workload released by individual vertices in the task graph. The interdependencies among vertices connected by edges are automatically guaranteed, as long as each vertex executes in the time interval defined by its artificial release time and deadline. A proper decomposition strategy can potentially smoothen the task's workload and thus improve the system schedulability. However, on the other hand, the resulting sporadic tasks' relative deadlines are much shorter than the original task, which may hurt the schedulability. Ideally, one can enumerate all the possible options for task decomposition for each concrete task set to get the best possible real-time performance, which is computationally unrealistic. The challenge is how to design efficient decomposition strategies to foster the strengths and circumvent the weaknesses of decomposition-based scheduling, and provide good schedulability in general.

In this paper, we proposed a new decomposition-based GEDF scheduling algorithm. In particular, we develop a new decomposition strategy that balances the strengths and weaknesses of decomposition-based scheduling with a simple metrics called structure characteristic value. This metric can very well represent a task's structure feature, and provide a clear guidance for the task decomposition procedure to achieve better schedulability. We developed decomposition strategies that are optimal respect to this metric. Moreover, this metric can be directly used for checking the schedulability of a task set, as well as quantifying the suboptimality (with capacity augmentation bounds) of our scheduling algorithm/analysis.

We conduct experiments with randomly generated task sets to evaluate the real-time performance, in terms of acceptance ratio, of our proposed scheduling algorithm and compare it with the state-of-the-art of, not only decompositionbased scheduling, but also global scheduling and federated scheduling. Comprehensive experiment results show that our algorithm is consistently superior to previous approaches in all of the three scheduling paradigms under different parameter settings.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: We consider the scheduling problem of a task set τ consisting of n periodic tasks {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }, executed on m identical processors. Each task is represented by a DAG, which is released periodically with a period T i . We assume all tasks to be implicit-deadline, i.e., the workload released by a task at time t must be finished by the next release time t + T i .

Each task τ i is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) consisting of several vertices and edges connecting them. With a slight abuse of notations, we sometimes also use τ i to denote the set of vertices in the corresponding DAG, A vertex v ∈ τ i has a worst-case execution time c(v). Edges represent dependencies among vertices. A directed edge from vertex v to u means that u can only be executed after v is finished. In this case, v is a predecessor of u, while u is a successor of v.
The total execution time of all vertices of task τ i is denoted by C i = v∈τi c(v). The utilization U i of a task τ i and the total utilization U of the task set τ are defined as follows
div.formula: U i = C i T i , U (τ ) = τi∈τ U i (1
div.p: L i denotes the sum of c(v) of each vertex v on the longest chain (also called the critical path) of task τ i , i.e., the execution time of the task τ i to be exclusively executed on infinite number of cores. The laxity of task τ i is T i -L i . We use Γ i to denote the elasticity of task τ i , which is defined as
div.formula: Γ i = L i T i
div.p: Figure 1 shows a DAG task example with 8 vertices. The utilization of this task is C i /T i = 30/25, the laxity is T i -L i = 10 and the elasticity is L i /T i = 15/25. Apparently if a task set τ is schedulable on m processors the following necessary conditions must hold:
div.formula: ∀τ i ∈ τ : L i ≤ T i , and τi∈τ U i ≤ m;

div.p: The target of task decomposition is to assign an artificial release time and deadline to each vertex (relative to the release time of the entire task), such that the dependencies among different vertices are automatically guaranteed as long as each individual vertex respects its own release time and deadline constraints.
We use d(v) to denote the relative deadline of a vertex v in a decomposed task, and the density of this vertex is
div.formula: δ(v) = c(v) d(v)

div.formula: i = max t>0 dbf i (t) t (3
div.p: The above defined demand bound function and load are natural generalizations of their correspondence for sequential sporadic tasks [10]. In practise, both dbf i (t) and i can be calculated in polynomial time. However, their actual calculation methods are not of our interests since they are merely used as auxiliary concepts in this paper and our scheduling and analysis techniques do not really need to compute them.

This schedulability test is independent on the specific task decomposition strategy in use. However, different decomposition strategies may lead to different values of and δ . A parallel task set may pass the schedulability test (4) with one decomposition strategy, but fail with another. Therefore, the target of this paper is to design good decomposition strategies, to minimize both and δ , and thus increase the chance for a task set to be deemed schedulable.

div.head: III. NEW DECOMPOSITION STRATEGY
div.p: This section introduces our new decomposition strategy, which consists of two major steps: (i) segmentation and (ii) laxity distribution. In the segmentation step, we divide the time window between two successive release times of τ i (the length is T i ) into several segments, and assign the workload of each vertex into these segments (a vertex may be split into several parts and each part is assigned to a different segment, as will be introduced later). In the laxity distribution step, the laxity T i -L i of this task is distributed into each segment, and thus given to the vertices in each segment accordingly.

The overall target of our decomposition strategy is to make the load of each segment and maximal density of its contained vertices to be as uniform as possible, and thus to minimize both the load and the maximal density among all vertices.

In Section III-A, we introduce the basic concepts of the segmentation phase. Before presenting our new segmentation strategy, we first introduce our laxity distribution strategy and related properties in Section III-B, after which it will become clear how the segmentation strategy affects the schedulability of a task set. Then we present our new segmentation strategy in Section III-C. Finally, Section III-D shows how different parts of a vertex assigned to different segments can be reassembled and scheduled as an entire entity at runtime, without violating the desired workload and density bounds.

div.head: C. Second Look into Segmentation
div.p: We use an ordered list S to store the vertices that have not been assigned to any segment, and use S x to store the vertices that have already been assigned to segment s x . Initially, S contains all the vertices of τ i , and each S x is empty. The elements in S are ordered in the increasing order of their latest finish times (ties are broken arbitrarily). The elements in S will be moved to each S x at the end of the segmentation procedure. The pseudo-code of our segmentation algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1, which consists of three phases: Phase 1: Assign each vertex that only covers a single segment. This phase is from line 1 to 5 in Algorithm 1. Each vertex that covers only one segment s x is simply moved from S to S x .

Phase 2: Assign the the remaining vertices to light segments as much as possible, without turning any light segment into heavy. This phase is from line 6 to 18. In this phase, we do assignment to each light segments one by one, in the time order (line 6). For each light segment s x , we assign vertices that cover s x , according to their order in S. A vertex u can be entirely assigned to segment s x if s x still remains light after added in the execution time of u (line 8). In this case, we move u from S to S x (9), and go into the next iteration, to assign the next vertex in S that covers s x . Otherwise, we split u into two parts u and u such that after adding u to s x , c(s x ) exactly reaches C i /L i , which is the threshold for being transformed from a light segment to a heavy one. In this case, the vertex assignment to the current segment is over, and we put the remaining part u back to S for future assignment to later segments. Phase 3: Assign the remaining vertices, if any, to the heavy segments arbitrarily. This phase is from line 19 to 21. After Phase 2, the remaining elements in S can only be assigned to heavy segments (including those segments that just reach the threshold in Phase 2). Since Ω i only depends on the total execution time in all heavy segments (i.e., C H i ), we can assign a remaining element in S to its covered segments arbitrarily. The only constraint is that the part of a vertex assigned to a segment s x is at most e(s x ).

div.head: D. Vertex Reassembling
div.p: The above segmentation procedure may split a vertex into several parts and each of them is assigned to a different segment. However, at runtime we do not need to schedule them individually. Instead, we will treat the entire vertex as a scheduling entity. Recall that initially the segments are divided according to the earliest ready time rdy(v) of vertices (which are also the latest finish time of vertices). As the segments are "sketched" in the step of laxity distribution, we will adjust these time constraints accordingly and use them as the vertex release time and deadlines. have been adjusted when the segment is "sketched" in the laxity distribution step).

V. EVALUATIONS

In this section, we evaluate our proposed decomposition algorithm by experiments. In particular, we will compare the acceptance ratio of our proposed algorithm and schedulability test, denoted by D-OUR with the state-of-the-art of all the three paradigms:

• Decomposition-based scheduling: We compare with the EDF-based scheduling algorithm and analysis techniques developed in [1], denoted by D-SAI. • Global scheduling: We compare with the following analysis methods in this category:

-The schedulability test based on workload analysis for GEDF in [5], denoted by G-BAR. -The schedulability test based on capacity augmentation bounds for GEDF in [7], denoted by G-LI. -The schedulability test based on response time analysis for GEDF in [6], denoted by G-MEL. Note that G-MEL was developed for a more general conditional DAG task mode. However, it can be directly applied to the DAG model of this paper, which is a special case of the one in [6].

• Federated scheduling: We compare with the schedulability test based on capacity augmentation bounds in [7], denoted by F-LI. Other methods not included in our comparison are either theoretically dominated or shown to be significantly outperformed (with empirical evaluations) by one of the above listed methods.

The task sets are generated using the Erdös-Rényi method G(n i , p) [13]. For each task, the number of vertices is randomly chosen in the range [50, 250] and the worst-case execution time of each vertex is randomly picked in the range [50, 100], and a valid period is generated according to its target utilization. For each possible edge we generate a random value in the range [0, 1] and add the edge to the graph only if the generated value is less than a predefined threshold p. In general the critical path of a DAG generated using the Erdös-Rényi method becomes longer as p increases, which makes the task more sequential. We compare the acceptance ratio of each of the methods. The acceptance ratio is the ratio between the number of task sets deemed to be schedulable by a method and the total number of task sets that participate in the experiment (with a specific parameter configuration).

Figure 5 shows the acceptance ratios of different methods under different normalized utilization (U /m) of the task sets, with m = 8, n = 5 and p = 0.01. The experiment results show that our method D-OUR clearly outperforms all the others. The breakdown normalized utilization of D-OUR is around 0.6, while is below 0.5 for all the others.

Figure 6 shows acceptance ratios with different number of processors, with a fixed number of tasks in each set n = 5, p = 0.01 and the total utilization U of each task set being 3. Similar to Figure 5, p is also randomly chosen from the its candidate set. Since the total workload is fixed now, it becomes easier to successfully schedule a task set with more processors. The experiment results show that D-OUR requires less processors than all the others to make the task sets to be schedulable.

Figure 7 shows acceptance ratios under different p (which determines the parallelism of tasks), with U = 3, n = 5 and m = 8. We can observe that for all the methods, the schedulability is better for tasks with higher parallelism. This is because, for a task with fixed total amount of workload, a more parallel structure in general leads to a shorter critical path, and thus more laxity, which is beneficial to schedulability. Since the trend of methods of different paradigms is the same, we can conclude that the effect of parallelism to schedulability is inherent to the parallel task model, but not the caused by any of these particular scheduling methods. Figure 7 shows the superiority of our method D-OUR over others with different parallelism degrees. Note that in this group of experiments, no task set is deemed schedulable by D-SAI or G-BAR. In order to reflect the differences of various value of p among the approaches with better acceptance ratio, we choose task sets with relatively high utilization. This is consistent with the results in the previous two figures. For example, the parameter setting of task sets with p = 0.01 in Figure 7 is the same as task sets with m = 8 in Figure 6. The corresponding acceptance ratios of each method with this particular setting are basically the same in two figures.
In summary, D-OUR consistently outperforms other methods in all the above experiments with varying parameters in different dimensions.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: Early work on real-time scheduling of parallel tasks assume constraints to task structures [14]- [17]. For example, a Gang EDF scheduling algorithm was proposed in [16] for moldable parallel tasks where the task could only be executed on a fixed number of processors. The synchronous task model was studied in [11], [17]- [22].

Recently, the scheduling problem of multiple DAGs has been studied with decomposition-based algorithms. In [1], a capacity augmentation bound of 4 was proved under GEDF. A schedulability test in [2] was provided to achieve a lower capacity bound than 4 in most cases, while in other cases above 4. In [3], a capacity bound of 3+ √ 5 2 was proved for some special task sets.

For global scheduling without decomposition, a resource augmentation bound of 2 was proved in [23] for a single arbitrary-deadline DAG task. In [4], [12], a resource augmentation bound of 2-1/m and a capacity augmentation bound of 4-2/m were proved. A pseudo-polynomial time sufficient schedulability test was presented in [4], which later was generalized and dominated by [5]. [12] proved the capacity augmentation bound 3+ √ 5 2

for GEDF and 3.732 for GRM. For federated scheduling, [12] provided a capacity augmentation bound of 2 for implicit-deadline tasks. In [24] a schedulability test for arbitrary deadline DAG was derived based on response-time analysis.
Beyond DAG task models, researchers have studied conditional parallel real-time tasks where both fork-join and branching semantics exist in the same graph [5], [6], [9].

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we study the scheduling of parallel real-time tasks modeled by DAG. We proposed a new decomposition algorithm under the guideline of the structure characteristic value of each task. The structure characteristic value can very well represent the feature of a task's structure, and be directly used to test the schedulability of the task set and quantify the suboptimality of our methods in terms of capacity augmentation bounds. Experiments with randomly generated task sets show that our proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art of, not only decomposition-based scheduling but also the other two paradigms, global scheduling and federated scheduling, under different parameter settings.

Note that although experimental results in this paper show clear superiority of our algorithm to the state-of-the-art of the all the three scheduling paradigms, we by no means claim the victory of decomposition-based scheduling against them. Instead, we believe the competition among them will continue, until the strength and weakness of each of them have been fully understood. Moreover, the final winner will very likely be a combination of these three paradigms that utilizes the best of their advantages. This will be the direction of our future work. Another possible future work is to extend decomposition-base scheduling to the conditional DAG task model.
